steps.intent: China's objective is to uphold a comprehensive approach to outer space security by reaffirming Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty while expanding commitments to prohibit the placement of all weapons in outer space and prevent an arms race through legally binding multilateral negotiations. We anticipate intense resistance from Western permanent members, particularly the United States and the United Kingdom, who reject references to legally binding instruments such as the draft PPWT and oppose expanding the draft beyond the narrow scope of weapons of mass destruction. Securing the necessary nine affirmative votes while avoiding a Western veto will be the primary diplomatic challenge given deep geopolitical divisions on space weaponization.

messages.Algeria: Algeria fully supports this draft resolution, which reflects our steadfast commitment to the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects, going beyond weapons of mass destruction. We welcome the reaffirmation of outer space as the province of all humankind and the emphasis on the Conference on Disarmament negotiating a comprehensive, legally binding instrument. We urge all Council members to engage constructively to ensure outer space is preserved exclusively for peaceful purposes for the benefit of all nations.
messages.Ecuador: Ecuador reaffirms its principled and consistent commitment to the exclusively peaceful use of outer space and strongly opposes its militarization and the placement of any type of weapons in orbit. In line with our previous votes, we support the urgent negotiation of legally binding instruments to prevent an arms race in outer space. To avoid further politicization and foster the broadest possible consensus among Council members, we suggest ensuring OP4 is inclusive of all relevant multilateral initiatives and proposals.
messages.France: France cannot support this draft, which appears designed to divert attention from the veto cast last month against a clear, urgent text reaffirming the prohibition of weapons of mass destruction in outer space. The draft seeks to legitimize the long-standing draft PPWT, which remains fundamentally unviable due to its lack of verification provisions and its failure to cover ground-based anti-satellite capabilities. Progress on outer space security requires strict adherence to existing obligations under the Outer Space Treaty and the pragmatic promotion of norms of responsible behaviours.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the draft resolution, which aligns with our principled position on the peaceful use of outer space and the urgent need to prevent the placement of weapons of any kind in this domain. Outer space is the province of all humankind and must be preserved strictly for peaceful purposes through multilateral cooperation and adherence to existing international legal frameworks. We encourage the penholders and all Council members to engage constructively to bridge differences and foster consensus on this critical global security issue.
messages.Japan: Japan remains fully committed to preserving outer space as a peaceful domain, but this draft attempts to revive the draft PPWT, which lacks effective verification mechanisms and ignores critical capabilities such as ground-launched anti-satellite missiles. Furthermore, this initiative appears to be an effort to deflect attention from the Russian Federation's veto of the widely supported Japan-US draft resolution (S/2024/302) on preventing the placement of weapons of mass destruction in outer space. Japan cannot support this text unless our fundamental concerns regarding verification, scope, and the mandate of negotiating forums are comprehensively addressed.
messages.Malta: Malta remains firmly committed to the preservation of outer space for peaceful purposes and the prevention of an arms race in outer space. However, this draft text duplicates initiatives that lack consensus and fails to address the essential requirements of verifiability and transparency, while referencing a flawed draft treaty. We urge the penholders to pursue a balanced and constructive approach that incorporates norms of responsible state behaviour rather than advancing a divisive text.
messages.Mozambique: Mozambique reaffirms its principled commitment to the preservation of outer space as a global commons dedicated exclusively to peaceful purposes and the province of all humankind. We fully support efforts aimed at preventing an arms race in outer space, including the prohibition of the placement of weapons of any kind in orbit. We encourage all Council members to engage constructively in good faith to bridge differences and strengthen the multilateral disarmament architecture.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea cannot support this draft resolution, which seeks to reintroduce language from the amendment that was already rejected by the Council last month following the veto of draft resolution S/2024/302. The draft promotes the fundamentally flawed draft PPWT, which lacks effective verification mechanisms and ignores ground-based anti-satellite capabilities. Rather than advancing divisive and unviable legally binding initiatives, the international community should focus on compliance with existing obligations under the Outer Space Treaty and developing norms of responsible state behavior.
messages.Russian Federation: As a co-sponsor of this draft resolution, the Russian Federation fully supports the text as presented. This draft provides a truly balanced and comprehensive approach to the prevention of an arms race in outer space by addressing not only weapons of mass destruction, but weapons of any kind, as well as the threat or use of force in and from space. We call on all Council members to support this initiative to ensure outer space remains exclusively peaceful.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone supports the draft resolution and reaffirms that outer space is a global commons that must remain strictly reserved for peaceful exploration and the benefit of all humankind. In line with our established principles on outer space security, we emphasize the necessity of including effective verification mechanisms within future legally binding instruments to prevent an arms race and militarization. We urge all delegations to engage constructively and bridge divides so the Council can act collectively on this vital issue.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia remains deeply committed to preventing an arms race in outer space, but this initiative appears to be an attempt to deflect attention from the recent veto of draft resolution S/2024/302. The current draft promotes the Sino-Russian draft PPWT, which lacks consensus, ignores ground-based anti-satellite systems, and completely lacks verification mechanisms. Unless the text genuinely reflects existing international legal obligations under the Outer Space Treaty and addresses practical, verifiable space security threats, Slovenia cannot support it.
messages.Switzerland: Switzerland remains firmly committed to the prevention of an arms race in outer space and supports the development of legally binding instruments that prohibit the placement of any weapons in space. However, to build genuine security and consensus, the Council must recognize the complementarity between legally binding measures and voluntary norms of responsible behaviour, and address all threats to space systems, including ground-based capabilities. We encourage the penholders to remove exclusive references to drafts that lack broad support and work towards a balanced, inclusive text.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom cannot support this draft text, which represents a disingenuous attempt to divert attention from the Russian Federation's veto of draft resolution S/2024/302 on upholding the Outer Space Treaty. The current draft inappropriately attempts to force consideration of the deeply flawed, unverifiable, and long-stalled draft PPWT, while completely ignoring ground-based anti-satellite threats. Effective progress on space security must focus on verifiable measures and the development of norms, rules, and principles of responsible space behaviours rather than divisive and one-sided texts.
messages.United States of America: This text is a transparent attempt by the sponsors to distract from Russia's indefensible veto last month of the United States and Japan's straightforward draft resolution upholding the Outer Space Treaty. The United States cannot support proposals that promote the fundamentally flawed and unverifiable draft PPWT or impose sweeping, undefined bans on 'weapons of any kind' while ignoring the immediate threat of WMD placement in orbit. If the sponsors are serious about outer space security, they should commit to not placing or developing nuclear weapons designed for orbit rather than advancing politicized and unworkable initiatives.

The text maintains the fundamental, comprehensive approach to preventing an arms race in outer space in all its aspects, preserving the prohibition of weapons of any kind and reaffirming the mandate of the Conference on Disarmament.

messages.Algeria: Algeria fully supports the current draft resolution, which reflects the longstanding aspirations of the Global South and the Non-Aligned Movement for the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. We particularly welcome the explicit call to prevent the placement of weapons of any kind in outer space and the emphasis on the Conference on Disarmament negotiating a legally binding instrument. We thank the co-sponsors for their efforts and stand ready to vote in favour of the text as drafted.
messages.Ecuador: Ecuador welcomes the incorporation of our proposal in operative paragraph 4, which ensures an open and inclusive approach taking into account all relevant initiatives on the prevention of an arms race in outer space. Consistent with our longstanding position against the militarization of outer space and our support for the development of legally binding instruments to preserve its exclusively peaceful nature, Ecuador supports the draft resolution as currently formulated.
messages.France: France cannot accept a draft that promotes the fundamentally flawed and unverifiable Sino-Russian draft PPWT, which fails to address key destabilizing threats such as ground-based anti-satellite capabilities. Any credible effort on space security and preventing an arms race in outer space must focus on practical, verifiable measures and the development of norms of responsible state behaviours. If these fundamental red lines and imbalances are not addressed, France will vote against this resolution.
messages.Guyana: Guyana reaffirms its principled commitment to the peaceful use of outer space and the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. We support the draft resolution, which rightly underscores that outer space is a global commons and the province of all humankind that must remain free of weapons. We appreciate the penholders' efforts and stand ready to support this text.
messages.Japan: Japan cannot support this draft, which disregards our core concerns and seeks to advance the flawed and unverifiable PPWT initiative rather than genuine, verifiable arms control in outer space. The text fails to address terrestrial threats such as ground-launched anti-satellite missiles while undermining established legal regimes and consensus-based mechanisms. Since our essential red line regarding the PPWT and our proposals on effective verification remain rejected, Japan will vote against this resolution.
messages.Malta: Malta regrets that our red line regarding the explicit reference to the draft PPWT in operative paragraph 4 was not accommodated, as this initiative lacks international consensus. We also emphasize that any meaningful text on space security must recognize the critical framework of norms, rules, and principles of responsible behaviours. In the absence of these vital adjustments, Malta will not be in a position to support this draft resolution.
messages.Mozambique: Mozambique reaffirms its full support for the draft resolution, which rightly emphasizes outer space as a global commons and the province of all humankind. We strongly endorse efforts to prevent an arms race and the placement of weapons of any kind in outer space, as well as the call to revitalize multilateral negotiations in the Conference on Disarmament. We are ready to support this text when put to a vote.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea regrets that our essential concerns were completely dismissed in the revised text. We cannot support an initiative that promotes flawed instruments like the draft PPWT, which lacks effective verification mechanisms and fails to address real, dual-use threats in outer space. Unless the text is rebalanced to prioritize practical, verifiable steps and norms of responsible behavior, the Republic of Korea will vote against this draft.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation fully supports the current draft resolution, of which we are a proud co-sponsor together with China. This text provides a comprehensive and balanced framework to keep outer space free from weapons of any kind and firmly upholds the mandate of the Conference on Disarmament to negotiate a legally binding instrument. We urge all Council members genuinely committed to peace in outer space to vote in favour of this draft.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks the penholders for positively considering and accommodating our request to incorporate reference to appropriate and effective verification mechanisms in operative paragraph 4. In line with our principled and consistent commitment to preserving outer space exclusively for peaceful purposes and preventing an arms race in outer space in all its aspects, Sierra Leone supports the draft resolution as currently revised.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia cannot support the draft resolution in its current form, as it remains fundamentally unbalanced and dismisses our core concerns. We cannot accept references to the draft PPWT, which lacks effective verification mechanisms and ignores key space-related threats, including ground-based anti-satellite systems. Any genuine effort to prevent an arms race in outer space must take a comprehensive approach, addressing all capabilities and recognizing the vital role of responsible space behaviours.
messages.Switzerland: Switzerland thanks the penholder for incorporating initial elements on verification and inclusivity, but we cannot support the draft in its current form. We have consistently maintained that the prevention of an arms race in outer space requires complementary approaches, combining legally binding instruments with voluntary norms, rules, and principles of responsible behaviours. Without adequate recognition of these complementary tracks and in the absence of a genuine consensus-building effort that bridges divisions in the Council, Switzerland will abstain.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom cannot accept a text that selectively promotes the deeply flawed, unverifiable Sino-Russian draft PPWT while ignoring Earth-to-space anti-satellite threats and the crucial work on norms, rules, and principles of responsible space behaviours. This initiative is a transparent attempt to divert attention from Russia's recent veto of the US-Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Outer Space Treaty. Unless these serious deficiencies are addressed, the United Kingdom will vote against this draft resolution.
messages.United States of America: This draft is a transparent, disingenuous distraction from Russia's veto of the straightforward US-Japan resolution and its ongoing development of a dangerous counterspace capability. By rejecting language calling on States not to develop nuclear weapons or other WMDs specifically designed for orbit, while promoting the inherently flawed and unverifiable draft PPWT, the sponsors reveal their true intentions. The United States cannot support this text and will vote against it if presented in this form.

steps.summary: China, acting in close coordination with the Russian Federation, maintains the draft resolution to ensure a comprehensive and legally binding approach to preventing an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. We reject Western attempts to excise reference to the draft PPWT, dilute disarmament commitments through non-binding responsible behaviours, or establish selective prohibitions that disregard wider space security threats. The draft firmly defends the mandate of the Conference on Disarmament and the shared interests of the vast majority of Member States.

before.Japan:
Japan will vote against the draft resolution before us today.

Just a few weeks ago, Japan, together with the United States, put forward a practical and timely draft resolution that reaffirmed the core obligation under the Outer Space Treaty not to place nuclear weapons or any other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around the Earth. That draft resolution received overwhelming support from the international community and sixty-five co-sponsors, yet it was vetoed by a single permanent member, the Russian Federation.

Today’s initiative, tabled by China and Russia, is not a genuine effort to advance outer space security. Instead, it seeks to divert attention from that veto and to revive long-standing, deeply flawed proposals, specifically the draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space (PPWT). Japan has repeatedly made clear our fundamental concerns with this approach: it lacks any verification mechanism, fails to address earth-based anti-satellite capabilities such as the destructive direct-ascent ASAT missile test conducted by Russia in 2021, and is fundamentally unworkable. 

Furthermore, our constructive proposals and red lines during consultations were entirely disregarded by the penholders. The Security Council cannot endorse an unverifiable and unbalanced text that undermines existing multilateral processes. For these reasons, Japan will vote "no".
before.Russian Federation:
Today, the Security Council has a real opportunity to take a comprehensive, balanced and constructive step toward preserving outer space as a peaceful domain for the benefit of all humankind. Together with the People’s Republic of China and our co-sponsors, the Russian Federation has submitted a draft resolution that addresses the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects.

Unlike the unbalanced and politicized initiative promoted last month by the United States and Japan, which artificially extracted only one element—weapons of mass destruction—from the broader architecture of space security in order to score cheap political points and vilify Russia, our draft resolution provides a genuine and holistic approach. It reaffirms existing obligations under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty not to place weapons of mass destruction in orbit, while crucially going further: it calls for urgent measures to prevent for all time the placement of weapons of any kind in outer space and the threat or use of force in outer space, from space against Earth and from Earth against objects in outer space.

Furthermore, our draft underlines the imperative of launching negotiations on a legally binding international instrument on the prevention of an arms race in outer space at the Conference on Disarmament, based on the draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space, the threat or use of force against outer space objects (PPWT). 

This draft reflects the long-standing demands and common aspirations of the overwhelming majority of the international community. Today’s vote will serve as a moment of truth. Those who claim to be concerned about the weaponization of space will have the chance to demonstrate their sincerity in deeds, not just in words. We urge all members of the Security Council to vote in favour of this draft resolution.
before.United States of America:
Today, the Security Council is being asked to vote on a disingenuous draft resolution tabled by Russia and China that does nothing to advance the security of outer space, but rather serves as a cynical distraction from Russia’s own dangerous and destabilizing actions.

Just four weeks ago, Russia vetoed a straightforward, balanced draft resolution put forward by the United States and Japan—a text that garnered broad support across the Council and would have reaffirmed a foundational principle of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty: that no State should place nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction into orbit. Russia’s veto of that text laid bare its true intentions and left the international community wondering what Russia might be trying to hide.

Instead of answering those legitimate questions, Russia and China have put forward a text that seeks to divert attention and revive their deeply flawed draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space (PPWT). As we have reiterated for years, that proposal contains no effective verification mechanisms, fails to address ground-based anti-satellite weapons—the very weapons Russia has already tested and deployed—and is entirely unworkable. 

The United States engaged in good faith and proposed reasonable edits, including calling on States not to develop nuclear weapons specifically designed to be placed in orbit. Those edits were summarily ignored. We will not support a hypocritical text that rewards Russia’s obfuscation, undermines real non-proliferation efforts, and seeks to rewrite established multilateral frameworks. For these reasons, the United States will vote against this draft resolution.

after.China:
China voted in favour of the draft resolution just put to the vote. We express our deep regret that the Security Council failed to adopt this draft resolution.

Outer space is a global commons that has a major bearing on the security and well-being of all humankind. Maintaining peace and tranquillity in outer space, preventing the weaponization of and an arms race in outer space, and promoting the peaceful use of outer space are shared aspirations and strong calls of the international community. 

At present, outer space security is facing increasingly complex and severe challenges. A certain major power defines outer space as an operational domain, vigorously develops space military forces, builds outer space military alliances, and continuously increases the risk of outer space weaponization and an arms race. Against this backdrop, taking practical measures to safeguard outer space security and prevent an arms race has become increasingly urgent.

The draft resolution just put to the vote was balanced, objective, and constructive. It reaffirmed the core provisions of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty and called on all States to comply fully with their treaty obligations, including not to place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction. At the same time, the draft resolution aimed to address the real threats to outer space security comprehensively, calling on all States, particularly those with major space capabilities, to take urgent measures to prevent for all time the placement of weapons of any kind in outer space and the threat or use of force in outer space, from space against Earth, and from Earth against objects in outer space. Furthermore, the draft emphasized the need for early negotiations on an international legally binding instrument on the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects at the Conference on Disarmament. 

Regrettably, certain Council members voted against this draft resolution. While claiming to support outer space security and the prevention of the placement of weapons of mass destruction in orbit, they persistently refused to address the placement of all types of weapons in outer space and opposed negotiating an international legally binding instrument. This fully exposes their true intention, which is to seek absolute military superiority in outer space for themselves while shirking their own non-proliferation and disarmament responsibilities.

China has always championed the peaceful use of outer space and firmly opposed the weaponization of and an arms race in outer space. Together with the Russian Federation, China submitted the draft Treaty on the Prevention of the Placement of Weapons in Outer Space, the Threat or Use of Force against Outer Space Objects (PPWT) to the Conference on Disarmament, which has received broad support from the international community. We will continue to work with all parties to firmly uphold multilateralism, actively advance the international legal process on outer space arms control, and make unremitting efforts to ensure that outer space remains a domain of peace, development, and shared benefits for all mankind.
after.France:
(spoke in French):

France voted against the draft resolution submitted by the Russian Federation and China.

Less than a month ago, on 24 April, the Russian Federation chose to use its veto against a draft resolution submitted by the United States and Japan, which had been co-sponsored by 65 Member States and supported by 13 members of this Council. That draft resolution simply reaffirmed a fundamental principle of international law and collective security: the prohibition on placing in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, in accordance with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.

Today’s draft resolution is not a genuine initiative to advance space security. It is a diversionary maneuver designed to distract from Russia’s isolated and unjustifiable veto, and an attempt to instrumentalize the Security Council.

France is firmly committed to preventing an arms race in outer space and preserving space as a peaceful, safe, and sustainable domain. However, the text put forward today seeks to promote a flawed draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space—the PPWT—which has shown its limits for over fifteen years. That initiative contains major shortcomings, particularly the lack of any definition of what constitutes a space weapon, the absence of an effective and verifiable verification regime, and the total disregard for ground-based anti-satellite weapons, such as direct-ascent missiles, which Russia itself tested in November 2021, creating thousands of pieces of dangerous debris.

Rather than pursuing divisive and unworkable proposals, we believe that progress can be achieved through concrete, pragmatic measures, including the development of norms, rules, and principles of responsible behaviors in outer space, as supported by the overwhelming majority of the General Assembly.

For all these reasons, France voted against this text.
after.Republic of Korea:
The Republic of Korea voted against the draft resolution contained in document S/2024/390.

Less than a month ago, the Security Council was presented with a timely, balanced and urgent draft resolution, submitted by Japan and the United States and co-sponsored by 65 Member States. That text simply reaffirmed existing legal obligations under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty and called on States not to develop or place nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. It enjoyed the overwhelming support of Council members, yet was vetoed by a single permanent member—the Russian Federation.

Today’s draft resolution, put forward by the Russian Federation and China, does not represent a genuine or constructive effort to advance the safety and security of outer space. Rather, it appears intended to deflect attention from Russia’s veto on 24 April. The text seeks to revive initiatives, such as the draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space (PPWT), which have been debated for decades without consensus due to fundamental and well-known flaws, notably the complete absence of effective verification mechanisms and the failure to address ground-based counter-space capabilities, including terrestrial anti-satellite weapons.

Furthermore, we cannot ignore the sheer irony that the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea appears as a co-sponsor of a draft resolution on space security. The DPRK has persistently violated multiple unanimous Security Council resolutions through its unlawful ballistic missile and satellite launches, directly threatening regional and international peace and security.

The Republic of Korea remains firmly committed to the peaceful use of outer space and to preventing an arms race in outer space. We believe that outer space must remain a safe, secure and sustainable domain for all humankind, and we will continue to actively support pragmatic and realistic efforts, including the development of norms, rules and principles of responsible behaviour in outer space.
after.Slovenia:
Slovenia voted against the draft resolution.

Just a few weeks ago, Slovenia supported the draft resolution tabled by Japan and the United States, which sought to reaffirm a fundamental principle of international space law: the obligation under Article IV of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty not to place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction. We deeply regretted the use of the veto on that text, which was a missed opportunity to strengthen our collective security and prevent the weaponization of outer space.

The draft resolution before us today does not represent a genuine and credible effort to advance the safety and security of outer space. Rather, it serves to divert attention from that veto and attempts to revive initiatives, such as the draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space, which have long been recognized as suffering from major structural shortcomings, notably the lack of a clear definition of space weapons and the absence of an effective, workable verification mechanism. 

Slovenia remains firmly committed to the preservation of outer space as a safe, stable and sustainable environment, free from an arms race, for the benefit of present and future generations. We believe that discussions on legally binding instruments must be pursued through inclusive, transparent negotiations in the appropriate multilateral disarmament bodies, primarily the Conference on Disarmament, on the basis of consensus and with verifiable mechanisms.

For these reasons, Slovenia could not support the draft resolution.
after.Switzerland:
Switzerland abstained in the vote on the draft resolution just considered by the Council. 

Preserving outer space as a peaceful, safe, stable and sustainable environment, free from an arms race, is a matter of vital importance for all humankind. Outer space is a global commons on which our societies, economies and security increasingly depend. 

Switzerland has consistently supported the objective of the prevention of an arms race in outer space in all its aspects. We remain firmly committed to the prohibition of the placement of weapons of any kind in outer space, including conventional weapons, and we support the development of a legally binding instrument to that end. We also continue to emphasize the complementary nature of legally binding instruments and voluntary norms, rules and principles of responsible behaviors.

Our commitment to these substantive objectives is unequivocal. However, achieving tangible progress in space security requires genuine dialogue, deep consultations and the building of broad consensus. We regret that this draft resolution was brought to a vote without the necessary consultations and collective engagement required to bridge existing divides. Rather than fostering trust and cooperation, the process surrounding this text has further accentuated polarization within this Council and diverted attention from substantive multilateral efforts.

The maintenance of international peace and security in outer space cannot be achieved through unilateral or divisive initiatives. It demands shared responsibility, mutual confidence, and constructive engagement across existing multilateral disarmament forums, notably the Conference on Disarmament and the relevant bodies of the General Assembly.

For those reasons, Switzerland chose to abstain. We urge all Member States, particularly space-faring nations, to redouble their diplomatic efforts and engage in constructive and inclusive dialogue to preserve outer space for peaceful purposes and for future generations.
after.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort:
The United Kingdom voted against the draft resolution before us today.

Less than a month ago, the Council had before it a straightforward, timely and widely supported draft resolution, put forward by Japan and the United States, reaffirming a core obligation of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty: that States must not place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction. That text was supported by thirteen members of this Council and sixty-five co-sponsors from across the globe. Yet it was vetoed by a single permanent member: the Russian Federation.

Today’s draft resolution was not a serious attempt to build consensus or advance the safety and security of outer space. Rather, it was a transparent attempt to divert attention from Russia’s veto on 24 April, which raised profound questions about its commitment to its existing international legal obligations.

Furthermore, the draft resolution seeks to advance long-standing, flawed initiatives—namely the draft treaty on the prevention of the placement of weapons in outer space. As we and many others have repeatedly pointed out, that proposal contains no effective verification mechanism and fails to address the full range of threats to space systems, including ground-based anti-satellite weapons, such as the one Russia tested in November 2021, creating thousands of pieces of dangerous debris.

The United Kingdom remains firmly committed to the prevention of an arms race in outer space. However, negotiations on legally binding instruments must take place in appropriate multilateral disarmament forums, with the full participation of the international community. Moreover, the United Kingdom continues to believe that the most practical and immediate way to prevent conflict and reduce threats in outer space is through the development of norms, rules and principles of responsible space behaviours.

For those reasons, the United Kingdom could not support this draft resolution.
after.United States of America:
I will be very brief.

The representative of the Russian Federation said that masks were torn off today. The mask came off on 24 April, when Russia vetoed a straightforward draft resolution reaffirming the fundamental obligation under article IV of the Outer Space Treaty not to place nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. 

Russia’s actions speak for themselves. No amount of disingenuous rhetoric or cynical draft resolutions can distract the Council and the international community from Russia’s true intentions and its dangerous veto last month. 

Thank you, Mr. President.
